title: charis
summary: The references connect divine kindness with grace, mercy, forgiveness, and a changed life, but they come from different linguistic and literary settings. Exodus 34, Psalm 103, and Micah 7 portray God as compassionate and forgiving in Israel’s Scriptures. Ephesians 2 describes people made alive by grace, and Titus 2 says grace trains its recipients for a godly life. These passages illuminate related themes; the Hebrew texts are not examples of the Greek term named in this entry.
historical_context: The set ranges from Israel’s narrative and poetry to prophetic speech and letters to Christian communities. Its Old Testament passages describe God’s compassion and forgiveness; Ephesians and Titus discuss grace in arguments about salvation and conduct. The listed sources do not support a more detailed lexical history.
canonical_context: Exodus 34, Psalm 103, and Micah 7 speak about God’s character and forgiveness in Hebrew Scripture. Ephesians 2 and Titus 2 describe grace in the context of new life and ethical formation. The connection is thematic and canonical, not a claim that the same Greek word occurs in each reference.
literary_context: Exodus records a divine self-proclamation, Psalm 103 is praise, Micah 7 closes with hope in pardon, Ephesians 2 contrasts death and new life, and Titus 2 presents grace as instruction. Their literary forms explain why the theme appears through confession, praise, hope, and exhortation.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect God’s mercy and forgiveness with the gift of new life and a changed way of living. The Old Testament references emphasize God’s compassion and faithfulness; Ephesians and Titus emphasize grace as gift and formation. Their relationship is meaningful without treating their distinct terms as interchangeable.
canonical_role: This entry brings together passages about divine compassion, forgiveness, grace, and transformed life. It distinguishes the Hebrew-scripture background from the New Testament discussions rather than treating every reference as a direct occurrence of one Greek term.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce charis to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
